item.title: Customer Service Is a Lesson in Learned Helplessness
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Customer Service Is a Lesson in Learned Helplessness

Personal Perspective: Unanswered requests can undermine your sense of control.

Posted November 19, 2026

When we contact customer service, no one actually helps us. We have come to expect this affront, even as it has reduced us to yelling uselessly into the digital void. While companies profit, we experience visceral harm.

Dog eat dog world
Source: Image by Wendy Lustbader

These repeated psychological defeats are not trivial. We may find ourselves putting off the chore of getting incorrect charges removed from a bill or promised service upgrades. Following the path of least resistance, giving up, saves us time and surges of outrage, but a subtle hit to our self-esteem is taken with each surrender.

Repeated blows to our sense of personal agency may be more consequential than we realize. When our calls for help are delayed or go unheeded, we may lose confidence that respectful consideration is even attainable. Dialogue with a chatbot or exchanges with an AI “assistant" keep us at an impotent distance that diminishes us.

Learned helplessness ensues

A few weeks ago, I dialed the customer service number because the service I’ve been paying for had stopped working. The customer service number on their website got me a mechanical voice at the outset: “If at any time you want to talk to a representative, say, representative." I said this word over and over, to no avail.

Not long ago, it was possible to speak to a person. These customer service people were effective, and the company made good on its promises. Now the obstructive methods tamper with our sense of control. No amount of persistence yields someone capable of correcting the problem and thus affirming our conviction of personal efficacy, our belief that we can get something done on our own behalf. The lesson of helplessness is learned again and again.

Research from the American Psychological Association shows that people care less about how long they wait and more about feeling like the line is moving. However, an amorphous phone system doesn't inform people of where they stand in line. The customer service hold is related to learned helplessness; both are uncontrollable and involve repeated frustration. Any action an individual takes has no impact. When people repeatedly endure unpleasant events they cannot escape or control, they stop trying to change their situation. This is learned helplessness.

A hopeful tale recently appeared in The New York Times. A man called for help about erroneous charges on his hotel bill; he spent time going through the motions. For a long while, he got nowhere, and his time was utterly wasted. Then, finally, he reached a human who instantly corrected the problem. Ah, but this unnamed hotel company had messed with the wrong man. It turned out to be the commissioner of the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, and he is not taking this lying down, as the saying goes.

item.title: Pursuit of Excellence Elevates Everything for Everyone
item.description:
Education

Pursuit of Excellence Elevates Everything for Everyone

Research consistently shows that excellence requires continual commitment.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Research on expertise notes the value of commitment.
  • Achievements are advanced by unrelenting application.
  • The pursuit of merit and excellence is neither accidental nor arbitrary.
Source: kalhh / Pixabay

All the privileges we enjoy, whatever they may be, have never been, and never will be, shared equally. However, what is understood and shared equally are universal truths, such as the laws of physics, gravity, and even the constructs of meritocracy and excellence.

For example, to tune an instrument requires the application of excellence. Tuning an instrument can be achieved with the hearing of an individual and now also through the use of technology. Research into music training demonstrates that musical precision develops through structured learning, refinement, repetition, and neuroplastic adaptation (Merrett et al., 2013; Neves et al., 2022).

Irrespective of whether tuning is done by an individual or through technology, the purpose and outcome are the same: to ensure that the instrument is pitch-perfect. When this is achieved, it means that the pursuit and application of excellence have met the required standard of vibrational sound perfection.

Achieving and Maintaining Excellence Through Deliberate Practice

Research on expertise consistently demonstrates that, irrespective of discipline or circumstance, high-level performance can be achieved only through the personal application of deliberate practice, determination, continual refinement, perseverance, feedback, resilience, and ongoing error correction until the required standard of excellence is attained. Once achieved, the same process must then be applied unrelentingly to maintain excellence (Ericsson, 2004, 2008).

The media has recently reported that the pursuit and application of excellence, in the area of symphonic orchestration, may be considered secondary and/or even unnecessary. My immediate response was, and remains: How is this even possible?

Source: Kevin Palmer / Pixabay

Symphony orchestration has been considered one of humanity's most highly regarded sophisticated presentations of coordinated musical excellence, often referred to as high art.

Effects of Musical Training on the Brain

Neuroscience research has also shown that musical training produces measurable structural and functional neurological changes in the brain, which also helps to enhance auditory processing and support higher-order executive cognitive functions.

All of this also supports fine and gross-motor biomechanical and neuromuscular skill acquisition and motor learning development processes (Merrett et al., 2013; Neves et al., 2022; Schlaug et al., 2005; Zaatar et al., 2024).

If excellence is required to tune a single instrument, it becomes even more important when dozens or even hundreds of musicians must perform together. Such performance is not achieved by accident. Rather, it emerges from disciplined preparation, deliberate practice, feedback, determination, high-level focus, and the pursuit of increasingly complex and refined standards of intellectual and skill-based performance excellence (Ericsson, 2004, 2008).

The question, therefore, is not whether merit and excellence matter. The question is how any musical institute that depends (in absolutely immutable terms) on both individual and collective merit-based competence (to achieve and apply biomechanical and musical coordination, precision, and musical perfection) could consider removing the universality of excellence and meritocracy from its very purpose of existence (Ericsson, 1999, 2004, 2008).

How Excellence and Meritocracy Drive Progress Across Disciplines

Whether in music, science, engineering, medicine, education, sport, or any other field of human endeavor, excellence and merit remains a universal principle that helps individuals and societies improve outcomes, elevate standards, and drive progress that ultimately benefits everyone (Ericsson, 1999, 2004, 2008).

The pursuit of excellence and meritocracy is therefore not merely desirable; it is the mechanism through which successful outcomes become possible. Excellence is neither accidental nor arbitrary. Rather, it emerges from the pursuit and application of meritocracy, applied achievements, competence, unrelenting effort, continual refinement, and the disciplined pursuit of superior reproducible performance (Ericsson, 1999, 2004, 2008).

Excellence and meritocracy, therefore, is not an optional opinion. It is the universal principle through which advancement occurs and through which civilization continues to progress. The pursuit of excellence elevates everything for everyone.

item.title: 3 Signs Your Adult Child's Problems Are Draining Your Life
item.description:
Parenting

3 Signs Your Adult Child's Problems Are Draining Your Life

You can love your adult child without losing yourself in the process.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Excessive rescuing can fuel helplessness in both parents and adult children.
  • Your adult child's unwillingness may reflect limitations that you may not fully understand.
  • Parents can care deeply without carrying every one of their adult child's problems.

During a recent presentation for a local chapter of the National Alliance on Mental Illness, I spoke about the emotionally taxing challenges of overcoming helplessness when parenting struggling adult children. I emphasized a central theme I see play out in the parents I coach, those contending with the overwhelming realities of seeing their grown children struggle in heartbreaking ways. By this, I mean how easily it is for parents to ironically lose themselves when they attempt to help their adult children find their way.

For sure, challenges like serious mental illness, chronic avoidance, substance use, personality factors, and other challenges can limit what adult children can realistically handle on a day-to-day basis. From working with so many parents in these situations, I appreciate these challenges. But no matter what difficulties parents face, they deserve a quality of life that includes moments of calm, serenity, self-nurturing, and pursuing activities that give them some joy, too.

As I discuss in my book—ou Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!—parental guilt and excessive rescuing create a powerful one-two punch that results in a relentless, emotionally exhausting cycle. Here are three signs that you may be caught in this cycle.

1. Your Adult Child's Moods Drive Your Moods

The parents of struggling adult children I coach often tell me they can only relax when their child is having a good day. For many parents in these situations, their state of mind is hypervigilant, constantly waiting for the next outburst, demand, or emotional push-pull cycle from their adult child.

One of my parent clients said: "When my daughter is angry or disappointed, it's like a pit in my stomach." What does this mean for parents in these circumstances? The effects I hear: Checking their phones when out with friends or being otherwise internally preoccupied about when the next ball is about to drop. Related, one distinction I emphasized during my recent presentation was caring versus carrying. By this I mean reminding yourself that you can care deeply about your adult child's struggles without emotionally carrying all of them

2. You Work Harder on Their Problems Than They Do

Do you open your laptop and research job or volunteering possibilities, look for therapists, provide money, try to discuss finances, and offer what feels like seemingly endless suggestions? If this is you, you are not alone. Nor are you alone if you end up feeling depleted and even resentful. It is so seductive to fall into the rescue trap, but remember that rescuing today to relieve distress may come at the cost of your adult child's self-confidence. Alternatively, even small accomplishments can help your adult child feel less helpless.

When you feel that compelling urge to offer solutions to your adult child, instead of rushing in wearing your "first responder" uniform, try asking, "What's one small step you feel capable of taking?" And to help this land well, be curious rather than critical about what your adult child can realistically manage.

3. You Feel Guilty When You Set Boundaries

It can feel maddening when your adult child accuses you of being selfish or reminds you of mistakes made when raising them. Many parents confide in me that they back down in these situations because they fear losing the relationship. Well, I have some really big news for you. You can acknowledge your past parenting setbacks and mistakes without spending the rest of your days feeling like you have to keep paying emotionally or financially. Your adult child can validly feel disappointed in things you did as a parent, but that doesn't automatically mean you did everything wrong.

Final Thoughts

I hope you can come away from this post realizing that reclaiming your life does not mean abandoning your adult child. You have spent much of your life trying to support and help your struggling adult child. You are still entitled to build, live, and enjoy your own life as well.

item.title: When Anger Makes ADHD Harder to Manage
item.description:
ADHD

When Anger Makes ADHD Harder to Manage

The ADHD-anger cycle: how anger can derail focus and increase impulsiveness.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • An impulsive reply can turn a moment of frustration into an argument that leads to more anger.
  • When anger takes hold, it can make it harder to remember what you wanted to say.
  • Radical acceptance may help you listen more to understand.

Anger can lead to increasing symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). When a person is angry, it’s hard to sit still, which is already a symptom that many people with ADHD experience. When you’re angry, your mind can become clouded, leading to careless mistakes and not listening to others because you are distracted. Stan’s anger leads not only to issues in his relationship but also to impairments in functioning in the workplace.

At work, Stan interrupts others and talks too much, leading to difficulties with others when his colleagues oppose his proposals. His anger leads him to quickly blame others, and before he knows it, he’s accusing others of dropping the ball. What follows next might be called an “ADHD triple play.” Instead of a pitcher getting three players out on base, he alienates three of his colleagues in vital roles for ensuring timely completion of a project.

Stan’s anger, in part, creates the ADHD symptoms of talking too much and not waiting his turn or listening to others. These are symptoms of ADHD, showing how ADHD can exacerbate anger. He interrupts Rob without listening to him (not waiting his turn), insults Clara rather than listening to understand her perspective (not listening), accuses Lena of not responding to emails (talking too much), and doesn’t give her an opening to explain her higher priorities and apologize for the delay.

How ADHD Symptoms Lead to Anger

So, how do ADHD symptoms lead to anger? In Stan’s case, his ADHD often sets the backdrop for instigating his anger. At work, he doesn’t always listen closely to updates about current projects during check-ins with his colleagues. Because he missed information, he is more likely to accuse his colleagues of things they didn’t do or of dropping the ball on things they actually did do.

You may feel forgetful at times. You might be guilty of hearing what a colleague said but then forgetting who said it, and you may find yourself getting angry at someone who wasn’t even involved. Or maybe you have a habit of butting in on others' conversations. Impulse control is a defining feature of ADHD, so butting in on others can lead to harsh comments from others, which can make them more angry. Then, as your anger alienates others, you might increasingly find yourself on the outside of conversations. You may sense the walls others put up, which can increase your anger at feeling left out. People might tiptoe around you to avoid your anger. It can only take one blow-up for others to have their radar up in every interaction, creating uncomfortable dynamics. This can lead to not being able to let go of the anger, which interferes with focus and listening to others.

Breaking the ADHD-Anger Cycle

One way to stop this vicious cycle is to learn skills for feeling the anger without taking it out on others. A simple principle of practicing radical acceptance starts with knowing you can’t control other people’s behavior.

The recommendation to choose acceptance is fundamentally hard. Trying to change the other person means you have not accepted the person or the stark reality that while you can influence other people, you can’t change them.

This is so hard that it can take a lifetime to learn this lesson. There are stages of life where there are grey zones. If you have a rebellious teenager, how much can you accept behavior that can lead to serious consequences? There are clearly areas where you have influence and can work to change the other person, such as parenting, teaching, and coaching, where your job is to identify blind spots and work for change.

Research shows that radical acceptance helps people to reframe negative events, which likely strengthens their coping skills (Segal et al., 2023). Keep in mind, radical acceptance does not mean approving of other people’s behavior. You may have valuable contributions to make, but your ADHD symptoms may cause others to dismiss you as a hothead. If this leads to failing to be persuasive, you may begin to feel ineffectual, like no one is listening to you, which can fuel more anger and resentment. Radical acceptance can help you acknowledge how frustrating it is to feel dismissed and choose a response that gives your ideas a better chance of being heard.

item.title: We’ve Been Getting “Alpha” All Wrong—Here's What It Really Means
item.description:
Gender

We’ve Been Getting “Alpha” All Wrong—Here's What It Really Means

Science contradicts the popular notion of the "alpha male."

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • The concept of the "alpha" is often misunderstood and can have dire societal consequences.
  • From a zoological perspective, "alpha" is collaborative rather than isolative.
  • Reimagining the definition of the "alpha" might help reduce societal aggression and isolation.

Think of the first thing that comes to mind when you hear the term “alpha male.” Maybe you picture a John Wayne type or a Douglas MacArthur; maybe a "jock" or the captain of the football team; maybe even a criminal like Tony Soprano of the television show The Sopranos or Frank Underwood of House of Cards. When we think of the concept of the “alpha male,” we tend to imagine it having to do with rugged independence, aggression, and dominant behavior.

Popular belief has largely aligned with these archetypal depictions of the “alpha.” This view of masculinity as dominant, aggressive, and hyper-independent is widely held across the globe, from the concept of the “man box” in Australia, which describes seven principles of being a man (self-sufficiency, acting tough, physical attractiveness, rigid gender roles, heterosexuality and homophobia, hypersexuality, aggression and control) to the “manosphere,” a loosely connected network of online communities that promote rigid, often unhealthy, views of manhood that align with the “alpha” concept (MensLine Australia, 2022).

But ironically, natural science contradicts this rigid interpretation of the “alpha” concept. While popular culture and media have depicted the “alpha male” in a way that has become widely accepted and unchallenged, zoology directly contradicts the notion that alphas are aggressive, dominant, and isolated. Early research on animal behavior spawned the concept of the “alpha male.” When zoologist Konrad Lorenz studied animal behavior in the 1960s to understand aggression in the natural world, he concluded that there were three hierarchical categories found in the animal kingdom:

  • “Alpha” = dominant leader
  • “Beta” = subordinate
  • “Omega” = lowest-ranking (Lorenz, 1966).

Lorenz’s conclusion implied that most animal behavior was predicated on aggression and dominance, and that animals were classified by either being dominant or submissive. This early animal research laid the foundation for what gradually became a widely held (yet oversimplified) belief about male behavior, with the “alpha” being seen as preferred and elite.

In the 1970s, however, biologist and expert on wolf behavior David Mech drew a very different conclusion than had Lorenz: the idea of the “alpha” had been oversimplified and misapplied in earlier research. Mech’s research revealed that wolf packs acted as family units, relying on cooperation and caregiving, rather than on fighting and aggression. The alpha role was actually taken on by both wolf parents, not just the male, to protect wolf cubs, ensure survival, and establish a family hierarchy (Mech, 1970).

Society often perpetuates myths that simplify more complex ideas: in this case, it is easier and simpler to view “alpha” as a singular personality type than to see it as a collaborative model that cannot be rigidly defined. The “alpha” concept has become so oversimplified that the way we tend to view it today is light years from its actual meaning in the animal kingdom. And the collateral damage of this misattribution has profound implications: A 2025 survey concluded that “young men ages 16 to 25 consuming online masculinity influencers’ content reported higher rates of emotional distress,” including feelings of worthlessness, nervousness, and sadness (Fischer, et al., 2025). A 2023 survey found that men in America are five times lonelier than they were in 1990, and, while finding a community is a necessity, not all communities—such as those like the “manosphere” are helpful or psychologically healthy (Bledsoe & Smith, 2025).

Despite the scientific debunking of the “alpha” myth, by the late 20th century, the idea of the “alpha male” had seeped into society and become widely accepted, as it remains today. We still hear this term used, and it is still thought by many to accurately describe “preferred” male behavior. Though it is often seen as describing qualities of leadership and success, the “alpha male” idea actually holds no scientific credence and is more a social construct than a fact of nature.

Survival in the animal kingdom is predicated upon collaboration, not isolation. A wolf pack is a “pack” for a reason—it would not survive without its collaborative dynamic. A “lone wolf”—though romanticized in popular culture and media—would actually struggle to get by without the support of a collaborative environment. It is no wonder, then, that when we rigidly view the “alpha” personality as being preferred, we run into countless problems, which can result in serious societal fissures such as a normalization of aggression, isolation, and unhealthy behaviors and responses. Taking a cue from nature might help us to reframe our often toxic definition of what “alpha” really means.

item.title: 'Not High, Not Drunk, Just Hungry'
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

'Not High, Not Drunk, Just Hungry'

Personal Perspective: A man on the street asks for help. Do we help?

Posted November 19, 2026

Hunger calls us. But do we answer?
Source: Steve Knutson/Unsplash

Just beyond the bridge, there’s a man in the middle of the roadway. He’s standing there on the thin divide between coming and going, speeding up to make the light and slowing down when it turns red, entering the city and getting out of town.

My daughter and I are leaving. The sun is sinking on another long day of work and school. If only my car could fly like the Jetsons’, we’d be home instead of inching along in this clogged line where the drivers’ aggravations rise like exhaust fumes into the twilight.

As we edge closer to the man, it’s the sign that grabs my attention. Simple. Clever. To the point.

Not High, Not Drunk, Just Hungry

That’s what it says as he waits, message in one hand, and a Whole Foods shopping bag in the other. Standing there on the thin divide between a warm car and a cold street, a full tank and an empty stomach, a way out and no way out.

If traffic were moving, I could just drive by. I wouldn’t have to look. I wouldn’t have to think. Stuck here in this jam, it’s not that easy.

He knows this. He’s smart. His little roadside marketing campaign has all the right elements. Know your audience. Address their concerns. Eliminate their objections. Appeal to their needs. Basic human needs. Food, water, that sort of thing.

The Whole Foods bag is a nice touch. Without a word, he’s telling us his intentions are good. Organic, pure and wholesome. And to think we might have suspected otherwise.

Motor running. Car stalled. Mind racing. Time suspended. I reach for my purse.

“Mom, you’re not going to give him money?”

My daughter’s words, yes. But they come from me, from what I’ve taught her over the years. Don’t talk to strangers. Don’t stop. Don’t get involved. You never really know who they are. You never really know where they come from. You never really know what they’re doing there in the middle of the roadway.

You never really know.

Especially now. In these hard times when the rules have all changed.

I roll down my window. The wind whips against my face as I hand the man a few crumpled bills I might have used for a cappuccino. He smiles. I search his eyes for something. Reassurance? About him? About me? The light turns green. We drive away.

But in my rearview mirror, I catch a glimpse of him alongside another car, another rolled-down window, another arm extended into the night.

As he waits.

Standing there on the thin divide between doubt and faith, cynicism and optimism, despair and hope.

Even if it is just one small ray.

item.title: When Your Cofounder Isn’t Who You Vetted
item.description:
Teamwork

When Your Cofounder Isn’t Who You Vetted

Good-faith answers can’t show how a partner will act under pressure.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Cofounder dating questions help, but answers reflect the values people hope to live by.
  • Under stress, people tend to fall back on older, less flexible ways of coping.
  • A multi-month work trial and cycles of rupture and repair are the best tests for a partnership.
Source: Dall-E / OpenAI

You’re driving home from the pitch, replaying the way your cofounder talked over you in front of the investor. The part that stings is that you did this carefully. You went through the cofounder dating questions together. You spent more time vetting them than most other founders you know. But you still ended up frustrated and disappointed, thinking to yourself: How did I choose wrong?

Most founders I work with put time and energy into selecting their cofounder. Many used Gloria Lin’s 50 questions, published by First Round Review. These questions are useful, but the problem is often that the answers were true when you gave them, and people change, especially under pressure.

Two founders I worked with demonstrated this clearly.

One of them was leaving an established company to start the business. Sarah was worried about what failing would do to her reputation and felt concerned she couldn't simply re-enter her role if she left. So she set a condition. She'd only make the leap if her partner, Tom, was willing to give up everything for the company: his sleep, his health, his marriage. Tom said yes, and he meant it (at the time).

Then Tom's wife got very sick. His priorities shifted, and he no longer wanted to prioritize the company above his marriage. He worked fewer hours. Sarah saw that as a breach of contract. Tom hoped that Sarah would change her mind and the two of them could keep building. But Sarah wasn’t willing to budge. She was quite clear on the level of sacrifice and commitment to the business she required, and they ultimately parted ways.

Looking back, the warning signs were present in their first conversation.

Sarah's demand was extreme. It highlighted unconscious anxiety about her inability to recover the prestige of her previous company and corresponding rigidity about sacrifice and commitment. The partnership agreement was also too inflexible. When Tom's life changed, they didn't have the capacity to change the terms.

Answers You Give on a Good Day

I find it useful to separate aspirational values from lived values. Aspirational values are the ones you’d list if someone asked you. Lived values are what someone watching your behavior would see.

When cofounders answer each other’s questions before they start, they’re mostly reporting aspirational values. They mean them. They just haven’t had to live them yet.

A core idea in psychoanalysis is that we’re of many minds, and that the conscious mind doesn’t always win.

Partnerships within a startup environment prove that point. Founders are often exhausted, sick, and under pressure, and in my experience, people regress under that kind of load. They fall back on older, less flexible ways of coping. It’s easy to say you’ll stay calm in a disagreement. It’s much harder when your heart is pounding, your revenue isn't growing, and you’re frustrated with the person across the table.

In a 1995 review in Psychological Bulletin, the psychologists Benjamin Karney and Thomas Bradbury drew on 115 longitudinal studies covering more than 45,000 marriages and proposed what they called the vulnerability-stress-adaptation model.

In their model, how a marriage fares depends on three things working together: what each partner brings into the relationship, such as personality and family history; the stress the couple faces; and how the two of them treat each other under that stress.

A couple can look steady when life is calm and struggle once the pressure rises. I see the same thing with cofounders, and a startup supplies plenty of pressure.

What Gets Left Unresolved

The second gap is specificity.

Two other cofounders I worked with had been colleagues at a previous company. Before starting, they agreed to a chart spelling out who was responsible for each area and who would be consulted or just informed on each decision.

The technical cofounder signed off on being informed about areas outside his own. What he actually expected was to be consulted, because to him that’s what being a cofounder meant. His partner saw the cofounder title as little more than extra equity. What mattered to her was running separate areas and moving fast. Nobody asked what “informed” meant, and the mismatch only surfaced once they were building.

Gaps like this tend to get pushed aside, because they feel less urgent than shipping a product or landing customers. Founders tell themselves they’ll talk once the demo works, then once they have more customers.

In my experience, the company usually grows faster than the partnership does. Whatever got skipped early comes back later, often at a bad moment, like the middle of a fundraise, when you’re also deciding who’ll be the face of the company to investors.

Testing a Partnership Before You Commit

The questions are a starting point. The test is working together long enough, ideally several months, to say yes to two things: We’re aligned on what we’re building, and I know how you act under stress. It helps to think in milestones rather than a set number of weeks.

The first yes covers the practical side: where you want the business to go, how you’ll fund it, what financial outcome each of you wants, how much risk each of you is taking on, and how much time and sacrifice each of you can give.

The second yes is about the two of you. Have you seen how your partner responds when things get hard, and do you still enjoy working with them? Can you give each other feedback in both directions? Have you had a genuine disagreement and come back from it?

That last one carries a lot of weight. In my work, trust between partners tends to grow through repeated cycles of rupture and repair, and the honeymoon period doesn’t offer many of those.

Before you sign anything, agree on how you’ll adjust equity, compensation, or roles if that were needed, and write it down. Most people’s life circumstances and values change at some point. What hurt the founders in my story was having no agreed way to adjust when that happened.

If you are successful, you'll spend the next 5 to 10 years with this person. Building resilience in a relationship requires going through hardship together and coming through aligned on the other side. There's no question that can preempt that.
